stem: Human capital refers to:
options: The stock of skills, knowledge, education, and good health embodied in the people (the human beings) of a country
solution: Human capital refers to the stock of skill, knowledge, expertise, education, training, and good health embodied in the people (the human beings/workforce) of a country — that is, the productive qualities and capabilities of the population. Just as physical capital (machines, buildings) is a source of production, human capital (the abilities and health of people) is a valuable resource that contributes to production and economic growth. Investing in people (through education and health) increases their productivity and thus builds up human capital. Understanding human capital (the skills/knowledge/health of people) is a key prelims point. Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge, education, and health embodied in the people of a country.

stem: Human capital formation refers to the process of:
options: building up/increasing human capital — through investment in education, health, training, etc., which raises people's productivity
solution: Human capital formation refers to the process of building up (increasing/developing) the stock of human capital in a country — that is, of improving and adding to the skills, knowledge, education, and health of the people. It is done through investment in human beings: investment in education, in health, in on-the-job training, in the migration of people (to better opportunities), and in information. Human capital formation raises the productivity and capabilities of the people, and hence contributes to economic growth and development. Understanding human capital formation (building up human capital) is a key prelims point. Human capital formation is the process of building up human capital through investment in education, health, and training.

stem: The two most important sources of (means of investing in) human capital formation are:
solution: The two most important sources of (or forms of investment in) human capital formation are education and health. Investment in education (schooling, training, higher education) increases people's knowledge and skills, raising their productivity; and investment in health (medical care, nutrition, sanitation) keeps people healthy and fit, which is also essential for them to be productive (a sick, weak person cannot work well). So education and health are the two chief pillars of human capital formation. (Other sources include on-the-job training, migration, and information.) Understanding that education and health are the main sources of human capital is a key prelims point. The two most important sources of human capital formation are education and health.

stem: Besides education and health, other sources of human capital formation include on-the-job training, migration, and:
options: expenditure on information (acquiring information about the labour market and other markets)
solution: Besides education and health, the other sources of human capital formation are: on-the-job training (workers being trained while working, which improves their skills); migration (people moving from one place to another — e.g., from villages to cities, or abroad — in search of better jobs and higher earnings, which involves a cost but raises their productivity/income); and expenditure on information — spending to acquire information (for example, about the labour market, wages, and educational and health institutions), which helps people make better decisions about their education, jobs, and so on. All these are investments that build up human capital. Understanding the sources of human capital (education, health, on-the-job training, migration, information) is a prelims point. Besides education and health, sources of human capital formation include on-the-job training, migration, and expenditure on information.

stem: Spending on education and health is regarded as an __________ (not merely a consumption expense), because it raises future productivity and income.
solution: Spending on education and health is regarded as an investment (in human capital) — not merely as a consumption expense or a burden — because, like any investment, it yields returns in the future: educating and keeping people healthy raises their skills, knowledge, and physical capacity, which increases their future productivity, earnings, and contribution to the economy. So money spent on education and health is not 'consumed and gone'; it builds up the productive capacity of the people (human capital), giving benefits (returns) over their whole working lives. This is why investing in education and health is so important for a country's development. Understanding that education/health spending is an investment is a key prelims point. Spending on education and health is an investment (in human capital), because it raises future productivity and income.

stem: Human capital contributes to economic growth because more educated and healthy people are:
options: more productive (and better able to innovate, adopt new technology, and add to output)
solution: Human capital contributes to economic growth because people who are more educated, skilled, and healthy are more productive — they can produce more and better goods and services, work more efficiently, and adopt and even create new technologies and innovations. Educated and skilled workers can use modern methods and machines, solve problems, and improve productivity; healthy workers can work harder and lose fewer working days to illness. So, by raising the productivity and capabilities of the workforce, human capital formation adds to the country's output and drives economic growth (and development). This is why human capital is regarded as a key source of growth. Understanding the link between human capital and growth is a key prelims point. Human capital contributes to economic growth because educated, skilled, and healthy people are more productive.

stem: Human capital and human development are related but not identical. Human development treats education and health as:
options: valuable in themselves — essential to human well-being and the ability to live a full life (ends in themselves), not just means to higher output
solution: Human capital and human development are related but differ in their perspective. The 'human capital' idea treats education and health mainly as a means to an end — as investments that increase people's productivity and hence economic output/growth (people are valued as a resource for production). 'Human development', by contrast, treats education and health (and a good life) as valuable in themselves — as ends in themselves, essential to human well-being and to every person's right and ability to live a full, dignified, and worthwhile life — regardless of whether they increase productivity. In the human-development view, every human being has a right to be educated and healthy, because that is essential to their well-being (not merely because it makes them more productive). Understanding this distinction (human capital = means; human development = ends/well-being) is a prelims point. In human development, education and health are valued as ends in themselves (essential to well-being), not merely as means to higher output.

stem: In India, the government body/ministry mainly responsible for education (which affects human capital formation) is the Ministry of __________.
solution: In India, the Ministry of Education (formerly called the Ministry of Human Resource Development) is the government ministry mainly responsible for education — for framing and implementing education policies and running educational institutions and programmes at the central level (with education also being handled by the state governments). Since education is a key source of human capital formation, this ministry plays a central role in developing India's human capital. (Similarly, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare handles health — the other main source of human capital.) Understanding which ministry handles education is a prelims-relevant point. The Ministry of Education (earlier the Ministry of Human Resource Development) is mainly responsible for education in India.

stem: India's spending (as a percentage of GDP) on education and health has generally been considered:
options: inadequate/too low (below the levels recommended and below those of many other countries)
solution: India's spending (as a percentage of its GDP) on education and health has generally been considered inadequate — too low, below the levels recommended by experts and policy documents (for example, the Education Commission had recommended spending at least 6% of GDP on education, a target not yet met), and below the levels spent by many other countries. This under-investment in education and health has been a shortcoming, limiting the development of India's human capital and contributing to problems like insufficient and poor-quality educational and health facilities. So a key issue is the need to raise the spending on education and health. Understanding that India's education/health spending is considered inadequate is a prelims-relevant point. India's spending on education and health (as a % of GDP) has generally been considered inadequate/too low.

stem: A major challenge for human capital formation in India is the widespread problem of __________ (a large proportion of the population being unable to read and write).
solution: A major challenge for human capital formation in India is the widespread problem of illiteracy (low literacy) — a large proportion of the population being unable to read and write. Although literacy has improved greatly since independence (from about 16% in 1947 to well over 70% now), a substantial number of Indians (especially among women, rural areas, and the poor) still remain illiterate, and the quality of education is often poor. Illiteracy and inadequate education hold back the development of skills and human capital, and hence the country's economic and social progress. Efforts like the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (aiming at universal elementary education) and the promotion of adult literacy aim to tackle this. Understanding illiteracy as a challenge to human capital is a prelims-relevant point. A major challenge for human capital formation in India is widespread illiteracy (low literacy).

stem: The government programme launched to achieve universal elementary education (education for all children aged 6–14) in India is the:
solution: The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) — meaning 'Education for All Movement' — is the major government programme launched to achieve universal elementary education in India, i.e., to provide useful and relevant elementary education (schooling) to all children in the 6–14 age group. It aims to get all children into school and to improve the quality of elementary education. (It is complemented by other schemes, like the Mid-Day Meal scheme to encourage attendance, and, importantly, the Right to Education — RTE — which made free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6–14.) Understanding the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (for universal elementary education) is a prelims-relevant point. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is the programme for achieving universal elementary education (for children aged 6–14) in India.

stem: The scheme of providing free cooked meals in government schools (which also encourages children to attend school) is the:
solution: The Mid-Day Meal scheme is the government scheme of providing free cooked meals (lunch) to children in government (and government-aided) schools. It serves two purposes: it improves the nutrition and health of the schoolchildren (helping their physical development and their ability to learn); and it encourages more children to attend and stay in school (by giving an incentive to come, especially to poor children, improving enrolment and attendance and reducing dropouts). So the Mid-Day Meal scheme supports both education and health — two key sources of human capital formation. Understanding the Mid-Day Meal scheme is a prelims-relevant point. The Mid-Day Meal scheme provides free cooked meals in government schools, improving nutrition and encouraging school attendance.

stem: The law (2009) that made free and compulsory education a fundamental right for all children aged 6 to 14 in India is the:
solution: The Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009 (the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act) is the law that made free and compulsory education a fundamental right for all children in the age group of 6 to 14 years in India. Under it, the state is obliged to provide free and compulsory elementary education to every child in this age group. (This followed the 86th Constitutional Amendment, which inserted the right to education as a fundamental right.) The RTE Act is a landmark in India's efforts to universalise elementary education and build human capital. Understanding the RTE Act, 2009 (right to education for 6–14) is a prelims-relevant point. The Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009 made free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14.

stem: A market-related problem in human capital formation is that the benefits of education and health cannot always be fully captured by the individual (there are 'external benefits' to society), which may lead to __________ investment if left entirely to the market.
solution: A market-related problem in human capital formation is that education and health generate 'external benefits' (positive externalities) — benefits that spill over to society as a whole, not just to the individual who is educated or healthy (for example, an educated person benefits their family, community, and the whole society through better citizenship, lower crime, healthier neighbours, etc.). Because the individual cannot capture (be paid for) all these social benefits, individuals (and the private market), acting on their own private gain, will tend to invest less in education and health than is best for society — i.e., there will be under-investment if left entirely to the market. This is why the government needs to intervene and invest in (and subsidise) education and health. Understanding this externality/under-investment problem (a justification for government role) is a prelims point. Because education and health have external benefits to society, leaving them entirely to the market leads to under-investment — justifying government intervention.

stem: The ministry mainly responsible for HEALTH (the other key source of human capital) in India is the Ministry of:
solution: In India, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the government ministry mainly responsible for health — for framing and implementing health policies and programmes, running public-health services and hospitals, and looking after public health, medical care, and family welfare (with health also being handled by the state governments). Since health is one of the two key sources of human capital formation (along with education), this ministry plays a central role in developing India's human capital. Understanding which ministry handles health is a prelims-relevant point. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is mainly responsible for health in India.

stem: The phenomenon in which highly educated and skilled people (like doctors, engineers, scientists) migrate/emigrate from a developing country to developed countries (a loss of human capital for the home country) is called:
solution: 'Brain drain' is the phenomenon in which highly educated, skilled, and talented people — such as doctors, engineers, scientists, and other professionals — migrate/emigrate from a (usually developing) country to the developed countries, in search of better opportunities, pay, and living conditions. This is a loss of valuable human capital for the home country (which had invested in educating and training these people, only to lose their skills and services to other countries). India has experienced brain drain (many of its talented professionals going abroad), though this can also bring some benefits (remittances, and, later, some returning with skills and investment — a 'brain gain'). Understanding brain drain (the emigration of skilled people) is a prelims-relevant point. 'Brain drain' is the migration of highly educated, skilled people from a developing country to developed countries, a loss of human capital.

stem: A regulatory body set up to maintain the standards of higher education (universities) in India is the:
solution: The University Grants Commission (UGC) is the statutory body set up to coordinate, determine, and maintain the standards of higher education (university education) in India. It provides grants (funds) to universities and colleges, and it lays down and monitors the standards and norms for higher education. (Similarly, there are regulatory bodies for specific fields — for example, the AICTE for technical education, the (former) MCI/NMC for medical education, etc.) These bodies help ensure and improve the quality of higher education — an important part of human capital formation. Understanding the UGC (regulator of higher education standards) is a prelims-relevant point. The University Grants Commission (UGC) maintains the standards of higher (university) education in India.

stem: There is a strong two-way relationship between human capital and economic growth: human capital promotes growth, AND economic growth:
options: provides the resources to invest more in education and health (further building human capital)
has no effect on human capital
solution: There is a strong two-way (mutually reinforcing) relationship between human capital and economic growth: on one hand, human capital promotes economic growth (educated, healthy, skilled people are more productive and drive growth); and on the other hand, economic growth in turn provides the resources (higher incomes for individuals, and higher revenues for the government) to invest more in education and health — thereby further building up human capital. So the two feed into each other in a virtuous cycle: more human capital → more growth → more resources → more human capital, and so on. This is why investing in human capital and achieving growth go hand in hand. Understanding this two-way relationship is a prelims point. Human capital and growth reinforce each other: human capital promotes growth, and growth provides the resources to invest more in human capital.

stem: The 'Right to Education' becoming a fundamental right, and the various education schemes, reflect the government's recognition that education is:
options: essential for human development and a right of every child (and vital for the nation's progress)
solution: The making of the 'Right to Education' a fundamental right (through the RTE Act, 2009, and the constitutional amendment), and the launching of various education schemes (like Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and the Mid-Day Meal scheme), reflect the government's recognition that education is: essential for human development (for every person's well-being and ability to lead a full life); a basic right of every child (not just a privilege for those who can afford it); and vital for the nation's economic and social progress (building the human capital needed for development, democracy, and equality). So education is treated as both a fundamental human right and a national priority. Understanding this recognition of the importance/right of education is a prelims-relevant point. Making education a fundamental right reflects the recognition that education is essential for human development, a right of every child, and vital for the nation's progress.

stem: Assertion (A): The government must play an important role in providing education and health. Reason (R): Education and health have large external (social) benefits and are essential to human development, so the private market alone would under-provide them, and the poor could not afford them. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the government must play an important role in providing education and health. And the reason is (R) that education and health have large external (social) benefits (they benefit society as a whole, not just the individual) and are essential to human development (a basic right and need) — so if left entirely to the private market, they would be under-provided (because the market ignores the social benefits), and, crucially, the poor could not afford to pay for them privately (so they would be excluded). Because of these reasons — externalities, the essential nature of education/health, and the inability of the poor to pay — the government must step in to provide (and subsidise) education and health for all. So R correctly explains why the government's role is essential (A). Understanding this justification for the government's role is a prelims point. The government must provide education and health because they have external benefits, are essential to human development, and the poor cannot afford them privately.

stem: A key difference between human capital and physical capital is that human capital is:
options: inseparable from its owner (the person) — it cannot be sold apart from the human being who possesses it
solution: A key difference between human capital and physical capital is that human capital is inseparable from its owner — the skills, knowledge, and health are embodied in the human being who possesses them, and cannot be separated from the person or sold apart from them (a person can sell the services of their skills, i.e., their labour, but not the skills themselves as a separate object). Physical capital (like a machine or building), by contrast, is separable from its owner — it can be sold, transferred, and used by others independently of who owns it. (Other differences: human capital is more mobile in some ways but restricted by nationality/culture; and human capital creates both private and social/external benefits.) Understanding this difference (human capital inseparable from its owner) is a prelims point. Human capital is inseparable from its owner (the person), unlike physical capital, which can be sold and transferred separately.

stem: Education can be broadly divided into formal education (through schools, colleges) and __________ education (informal learning outside formal institutions).
solution: Education can be broadly divided into: formal education — the structured, institutional education imparted through schools, colleges, and universities, following a set curriculum and leading to degrees/certificates; and informal (non-formal) education — the learning that takes place outside these formal institutions, such as through the family, community, work experience, self-study, adult-education programmes, and everyday life. Both contribute to a person's knowledge and skills (and hence to human capital), though formal education is the more organised and measurable form. Understanding formal vs informal education is a prelims point. Education is divided into formal education (schools, colleges) and informal (non-formal) education (learning outside formal institutions).

stem: The education of __________ is especially important, because it has powerful positive effects on the family, the health and education of children, and society ('educating a woman educates a family').
solution: The education of women/girls (female education) is especially important because it has powerful positive effects that go beyond the individual woman: an educated woman is better able to look after the health, nutrition, and education of her children (and family), tends to have a smaller and healthier family, and contributes more to the household income and to society. This is captured in the saying that 'educating a woman educates a whole family (or generation)'. So female education has strong intergenerational and social benefits — making it a high priority for human capital formation and development (and a means to greater gender equality). This is why raising female literacy and girls' schooling is emphasised. Understanding the special importance of female education is a prelims-relevant point. Female education is especially important because it strongly benefits the family, children's health and education, and society ('educating a woman educates a family').

stem: The Education Commission (Kothari Commission) recommended that India should spend at least __________ of its GDP on education.
solution: The Education Commission (the Kothari Commission, 1964–66) recommended that India should spend at least 6% of its national income (GDP) on education, in order to develop education adequately and build up the country's human capital. This 6% target has been widely cited (and reaffirmed in later policies), but India's actual spending on education has generally remained below this target — which is why the under-investment in education is a persistent concern. Understanding the 6%-of-GDP recommendation (Kothari Commission) is a prelims-relevant point. The Kothari (Education) Commission recommended spending at least 6% of GDP on education.

stem: The new education policy that replaced the earlier policy, aiming to reform India's education system (from school to higher education), is the National Education Policy (NEP) of:
solution: The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 is the new comprehensive education policy adopted by India to reform and transform the education system — from school education to higher education. It replaced the earlier National Policy on Education (of 1986/1992). NEP 2020 introduced several major changes and goals — such as a new school structure (the 5+3+3+4 system), an emphasis on foundational literacy and numeracy, flexibility and multidisciplinary learning, vocational education, the promotion of Indian languages, and a target of raising public spending on education toward 6% of GDP. Understanding NEP 2020 (the new education policy) is a prelims-relevant point. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 is India's new policy to reform education from school to higher education.

stem: Education/training that gives specific practical/job skills (like for a trade or occupation), rather than only general academic knowledge, is called __________ education.
solution: Vocational education (and training) is education/training that imparts specific, practical, job-oriented skills — the skills needed for a particular trade, craft, occupation, or profession (like electrician, mechanic, nursing, computer skills, tailoring, etc.) — rather than only general academic/theoretical knowledge. Vocational education is important for human capital formation because it directly makes people employable and productive in specific jobs, and it helps meet the economy's need for skilled workers. India has been emphasising the expansion of vocational education and skill development (e.g., through the 'Skill India' mission) to build a skilled workforce. Understanding vocational education (practical job-skills training) is a prelims-relevant point. Vocational education gives specific practical/job skills (for a trade or occupation), rather than only general academic knowledge.

stem: The national mission launched to train and develop the skills of India's large youth population (to make them employable) is the __________ Mission.
solution: The 'Skill India' Mission (National Skill Development Mission) is the government initiative launched to train and develop the skills of India's large youth population — to impart employable, job-relevant skills to millions of young people — so as to make them productive and employable, meet the skill needs of industry, and harness India's 'demographic dividend' (its large young workforce). It reflects the recognition that skilling the workforce (vocational training) is essential for human capital formation and for turning the youthful population into an economic asset. Understanding the Skill India mission is a prelims-relevant point. The 'Skill India' Mission was launched to train and develop the skills of India's youth, to make them employable.

stem: Health, as a source of human capital, includes preventive medicine (like vaccination), curative medicine (treatment of illness), and:
options: social medicine / public health (sanitation, clean water, spreading health awareness)
solution: Health, as a source of human capital, involves several dimensions of health care/expenditure: preventive medicine (measures to prevent illness — like vaccination/immunisation); curative medicine (the treatment of people who are already sick — medicines, hospitals, doctors); social medicine and public health (measures for the health of the community as a whole — like clean drinking water, sanitation, the control of epidemics, and the spread of health education/awareness); and the provision of clean drinking water and good sanitation. All these together keep people healthy and fit (physically able to work and be productive), thereby building human capital. Understanding these dimensions of health (preventive, curative, public health) is a prelims point. Health includes preventive medicine (vaccination), curative medicine (treatment), and social medicine/public health (sanitation, clean water, awareness).

stem: The basic health-care institution in rural India (the first point of contact for medical care in villages) is the:
solution: The Primary Health Centre (PHC) is the basic public health-care institution in rural India — the first point of contact between the village community and a qualified doctor/medical care. PHCs (and the sub-centres below them, and the Community Health Centres — CHCs — above them) form the backbone of the rural public health-care system, providing primary medical care, maternal and child health services, immunisation, and basic treatment to the rural population. The adequacy and functioning of PHCs are important for the health (and hence human capital) of rural India. Understanding the PHC (basic rural health-care institution) is a prelims-relevant point. The Primary Health Centre (PHC) is the basic health-care institution in rural India.

stem: A concern about health care in India is the heavy reliance on __________ (private) health expenditure, which burdens the poor.
solution: A concern about health care in India is the heavy reliance on out-of-pocket (private) health expenditure — that is, people having to pay directly, from their own pockets, for their medical care (doctors, medicines, hospitals), because public (government) health facilities are inadequate. This heavy out-of-pocket spending burdens the poor especially hard: a serious illness can push a poor family into debt and deeper poverty (medical expenses being a major cause of impoverishment). It reflects the inadequate public provision of health care and the low government spending on health. This is why expanding affordable public health care and health insurance (like the Ayushman Bharat scheme) is important. Understanding the burden of out-of-pocket health spending is a prelims-relevant point. A concern in India is the heavy reliance on out-of-pocket (private) health spending, which burdens the poor.

stem: Since independence, India's literacy rate has __________, but it is still not universal (and gaps remain between men and women, and rural and urban areas).
solution: Since independence, India's literacy rate has risen substantially — from only about 16% in 1951 to well over 70% in recent decades (crossing 74% by the 2011 Census, and higher since). This is a major achievement of India's education efforts. However, literacy is still not universal (a significant number of people remain illiterate), and important gaps/disparities remain — for example, female literacy is lower than male literacy, and rural literacy is lower than urban literacy (as well as gaps across states and social groups). So, while much progress has been made, more remains to be done to achieve universal literacy and to close these gaps. Understanding the rise in literacy (and the remaining gaps) is a prelims-relevant point. India's literacy rate has risen substantially since independence (from ~16% to over 70%), but it is not yet universal and gaps remain.

stem: The proportion of children who leave school before completing a given level of education is called the __________ rate — a problem in Indian education.
solution: The drop-out rate is the proportion (percentage) of children who leave school (drop out) before completing a given level of education (before finishing the class/level they had enrolled in). A high drop-out rate is a serious problem in Indian education: although many children enrol in school, a large number drop out before completing their schooling — especially at the higher classes, and more so among poor children, girls, and rural/disadvantaged groups — due to reasons like poverty (the need to work or earn), the cost of education, poor school quality/facilities, and social factors. Reducing the drop-out rate (retaining children in school) is an important goal (aided by schemes like the Mid-Day Meal). Understanding the drop-out rate (a problem in Indian education) is a prelims-relevant point. The drop-out rate is the proportion of children who leave school before completing a level — a problem in Indian education.

stem: Education and health are sometimes called 'merit goods' — goods that are so important that the government ensures their provision to all, because:
options: they are only for the rich
they are essential and beneficial to society, and everyone (including the poor) should have access to them regardless of ability to pay
solution: Education and health are sometimes called 'merit goods' — goods (and services) that are considered so important, meritorious, and beneficial (both to the individual and to society) that the government ensures their provision to all people, rather than leaving them entirely to the market. The reasoning is that these goods are essential to human well-being and have large social benefits, and everyone — including the poor — should have access to them regardless of their ability to pay for them. If left to the market, they would be under-provided and the poor would be excluded; so the government provides and subsidises them (treating them as merit goods that all deserve). Understanding education/health as merit goods is a prelims-relevant point. Education and health are 'merit goods' — so essential and socially beneficial that the government ensures access for all, regardless of ability to pay.

stem: India has one of the LARGEST higher-education systems in the world, including premier institutions such as the:
options: IITs (Indian Institutes of Technology) and IIMs (Indian Institutes of Management)
solution: India has one of the largest higher-education systems in the world (with a very large number of universities and colleges and millions of students). It includes premier, world-renowned institutions such as the IITs (Indian Institutes of Technology — for engineering and technology) and the IIMs (Indian Institutes of Management — for management/business), as well as top universities, medical colleges (AIIMS), and research institutions. These institutions produce highly skilled professionals and contribute greatly to India's human capital (and to its scientific, technical, and managerial capabilities). However, the higher-education system also faces challenges of quality, access, and relevance. Understanding that India has a large higher-education system (with IITs, IIMs, etc.) is a prelims-relevant point. India has one of the largest higher-education systems in the world, including premier institutions like the IITs and IIMs.

stem: The migration of skilled people abroad (brain drain) is a loss, but such migrants can also benefit the home country by:
options: sending back remittances (money), and later returning with skills, capital, and connections (a possible 'brain gain')
solution: The migration of skilled people abroad (brain drain) is a loss of human capital for the home country, but such migrants can also benefit the home country in several ways: they send back remittances (money earned abroad, sent home to their families), which are a major source of foreign exchange and income for the home country; and some of them later return with enhanced skills, experience, capital, and international connections/networks, which they invest and use to help develop the home economy (a phenomenon sometimes called 'brain gain' or 'reverse brain drain'). They may also help by transferring technology and knowledge, and by promoting trade and investment links. So skilled emigration has both costs (the loss of talent) and some potential benefits (remittances, and later return/linkages). Understanding these benefits (remittances, brain gain) is a prelims-relevant point. Skilled migrants abroad can benefit the home country by sending remittances and later returning with skills, capital, and connections (a possible 'brain gain').

stem: The key health indicators used to judge the health status of a population include the infant mortality rate, life expectancy, and the __________ rate.
solution: The key health indicators used to judge the health status of a population include: the infant mortality rate (IMR — the number of infant deaths per 1000 live births); the life expectancy (the average number of years a person is expected to live); and the maternal mortality rate/ratio (MMR — the number of women who die from pregnancy/childbirth-related causes, per 100,000 live births). Other indicators include the crude birth and death rates, the child mortality rate, and measures of nutrition and immunisation. These indicators reflect how healthy a population is (and hence the state of its human capital in terms of health); improvements in them (falling IMR and MMR, rising life expectancy) show improving health. Understanding these health indicators is a prelims-relevant point. Key health indicators include the infant mortality rate, life expectancy, and the maternal mortality rate (MMR).

stem: The health of the population depends not only on medical care but also greatly on __________.
options: nutrition (good food) and clean drinking water and sanitation
solution: The health of a population depends not only on medical care (doctors, hospitals, medicines) but also greatly on other factors — especially nutrition (adequate and good food, so that people, particularly children, are well-nourished and not weakened by hunger/malnutrition), and clean drinking water and good sanitation (which prevent water-borne and other diseases). Without good nutrition, clean water, and sanitation, people fall ill easily (no amount of curative medicine can substitute for these basics). So public health (clean water, sanitation, nutrition, hygiene, disease control) is fundamental to the population's health — and hence to health as a source of human capital. This is why programmes for nutrition, sanitation (like Swachh Bharat), and clean water are important for health. Understanding that nutrition/water/sanitation are vital to health is a prelims-relevant point. Health depends greatly on nutrition, clean drinking water, and sanitation — not only on medical care.

stem: Investment in education raises a person's future __________ (a private benefit that motivates individuals to acquire education).
solution: Investment in education raises a person's future earnings/income (and productivity) — this is the private benefit (return) that motivates individuals to acquire education. Studies generally show that more-educated people earn higher incomes (over their lifetimes) than less-educated people, because education makes them more skilled and productive (and gives them access to better-paying jobs). So, from the individual's point of view, spending on education is an investment that yields higher future earnings — which is why people (and families) are willing to invest in education. (This is the 'private return' to education, alongside the 'social return'/external benefits to society.) Understanding that education raises future earnings is a prelims point. Investment in education raises a person's future earnings/income and productivity — the private benefit that motivates people to get educated.

stem: The 'demographic dividend' that India can gain from its large young population depends CRUCIALLY on:
options: investing in the education, skills, and health of the young people (building their human capital) so they can be productively employed
solution: The 'demographic dividend' refers to the potential economic boost a country can get from having a large proportion of young, working-age people (as India does). But this dividend is only a potential — realising it depends crucially on investing in the education, skills, and health of these young people (building up their human capital) and providing them with productive employment. If the youth are well-educated, skilled, and healthy, and have jobs, they can drive rapid economic growth (the dividend); but if they are poorly educated, unskilled, unhealthy, or unemployed, the large young population becomes a liability (a 'demographic disaster') rather than a dividend. So human capital formation (education, skills, health) is the key to turning India's youthful population into an asset. Understanding that the demographic dividend depends on human capital investment is a prelims-relevant point. India's demographic dividend depends crucially on investing in the education, skills, and health of its young people so they can be productively employed.

stem: In India, expenditure on education is undertaken by both the __________ governments.
solution: In India, expenditure on education (and its provision) is undertaken by both the central (union) government and the state governments. Education is a subject on which both the centre and the states can legislate and spend (it is in the 'Concurrent List' of the Constitution). The state governments, in fact, bear a large part of the responsibility for education (especially school education), while the central government also plays a major role (in policy, higher education, and centrally-sponsored schemes). So both levels of government contribute to education spending — and the total government spending on education is the sum of the central and state expenditures. Understanding that both centre and states spend on education is a prelims-relevant point. In India, expenditure on education is undertaken by both the central and the state governments.

stem: The proportion of the population enrolled in education at a given level (e.g., higher education) relative to the eligible age group is measured by the __________ Ratio.
solution: The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) is the measure of the number of students actually enrolled in a given level of education (e.g., primary, secondary, or higher education), expressed as a percentage of the total population in the eligible/corresponding age group for that level. It is used to judge how much of the eligible population is participating in education at each level (the level of access/coverage of education). For example, the GER in higher education tells us what proportion of the college-age population is enrolled in higher education. Raising the GER (getting more of the eligible age group into school/college) is a goal of education policy. Understanding the Gross Enrolment Ratio is a prelims-relevant point. The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) measures the proportion of the eligible age group enrolled at a given level of education.

stem: A skilled and healthy workforce is important for a country because it can better absorb and use __________ (modern methods), raising productivity.
solution: A skilled (educated) and healthy workforce is important for a country because such workers can better absorb, understand, adopt, and use new technology and modern methods of production — and even develop new technologies and innovations themselves. Educated, skilled workers can operate complex machines, apply new techniques, adapt to change, and solve problems, all of which raise productivity and output. (Uneducated, unskilled, or unhealthy workers cannot make good use of modern technology.) So a country with high human capital can take fuller advantage of technological progress to grow faster — which is a key reason human capital drives economic growth. Understanding that a skilled workforce better uses new technology is a prelims point. A skilled, healthy workforce can better absorb and use new technology and modern methods, raising productivity.

stem: The government scheme providing health insurance/coverage to poor families for hospital treatment (to protect them from catastrophic medical costs) is __________.
solution: Ayushman Bharat — including its scheme PM-JAY (Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana) — is the government scheme that provides health insurance/coverage to poor and vulnerable families for hospital treatment (secondary and tertiary care), offering them free or cashless treatment up to a certain amount at empanelled hospitals. Its aim is to protect the poor from the catastrophic out-of-pocket medical costs that can push them into poverty (and to improve their access to health care). It is one of the world's largest health-insurance schemes. Such schemes address the concern about the heavy burden of out-of-pocket health spending on the poor, and they support the health dimension of human capital. Understanding the Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY) health scheme is a prelims-relevant point. Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY) provides health insurance/coverage to poor families for hospital treatment, protecting them from catastrophic medical costs.

stem: The 'social benefit' (external benefit) of an educated society includes:
options: a more aware, participative, and progressive society (better democracy, health, and social outcomes) — benefits that go beyond the individual
solution: The 'social benefit' (external benefit) of an educated society — the benefits that go beyond the individual who is educated, to society as a whole — includes: a more aware, informed, and participative citizenry (which strengthens democracy — educated people vote more wisely and hold the government accountable); better health and lower mortality in the community (educated people, and their families, tend to be healthier and adopt better health practices); lower birth rates and better family planning; less crime and social conflict; greater social awareness, tolerance, and progress; and an overall more advanced, developed, and civilised society. These wide-ranging social benefits (in addition to the private benefit of higher individual income) are why education is so valuable to society and why the government invests in it. Understanding the social/external benefits of education is a prelims point. An educated society brings wide social benefits — a more aware, participative, healthy, and progressive society — beyond the individual.

stem: The difference between the human-capital and human-development approaches matters because, in the human-development view, even a person whose education does NOT increase their productivity:
options: still has a right to be educated (because education is essential to their well-being and dignity, an end in itself)
solution: The difference between the human-capital and human-development approaches matters because of how they view a person whose education does not (or is not expected to) increase their productivity. In the pure 'human-capital' view (education as a means to productivity/output), educating such a person might seem 'not worthwhile' (no productivity return). But in the 'human-development' view, even such a person still has a right to be educated — because education is essential to that person's own well-being, dignity, and ability to live a full, informed, and worthwhile life, quite apart from whether it makes them more productive. In other words, human development regards education (and health) as valuable ends in themselves — a right of every human being — not merely as investments justified by their economic return. This is a crucial distinction. Understanding why the human-development view matters here is a prelims point. In the human-development view, even a person whose education doesn't raise productivity still has a right to be educated, because education is essential to their well-being — an end in itself.

stem: One reason for the slow progress of human capital formation in India has been the __________ of the population, which strains the provision of education and health for all.
solution: One reason for the slow progress of human capital formation in India has been the rapid growth (and very large size) of the population. A fast-growing, huge population puts enormous strain on the provision of education and health facilities: the country must keep building more and more schools, colleges, hospitals, and health centres, and training more teachers and doctors, just to keep up with the growing numbers — which is very difficult given limited resources. As a result, the available facilities are stretched thin, and it is hard to provide adequate, good-quality education and health care for everyone. So the population pressure has been a major challenge for developing India's human capital. Understanding population growth as a strain on human capital formation is a prelims-relevant point. The rapid growth/large size of India's population strains the provision of education and health for all, slowing human capital formation.

stem: In-service or 'on-the-job' training (training workers while they work) benefits both the worker and the firm because it:
options: raises the worker's skills and productivity (benefiting the firm's output and the worker's earnings)
solution: On-the-job training (in-service training — training workers while they are employed, e.g., learning new skills at the workplace, either on-site by working under experienced staff, or off-site in classes/institutes sponsored by the firm) is a source of human capital formation that benefits both the worker and the firm: it raises the worker's skills, knowledge, and productivity, which increases the firm's output and efficiency (benefiting the firm) and also raises the worker's own capabilities and earning potential (benefiting the worker). Firms invest in such training expecting the higher productivity to more than repay the cost. So on-the-job training builds human capital in a way that is mutually beneficial. Understanding on-the-job training (its benefits) is a prelims point. On-the-job training raises workers' skills and productivity, benefiting both the firm (output) and the worker (earnings).

stem: The National Health Mission (including the National Rural Health Mission) aims to:
options: improve the availability of, and access to, quality health care — especially for the rural and poor population
solution: The National Health Mission (NHM) — which includes the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and the National Urban Health Mission — is the major government programme that aims to improve the availability of, and access to, quality health-care services, especially for the rural population and the poor and vulnerable (and to strengthen the public health-care system, from sub-centres and PHCs upward). It focuses on areas like maternal and child health, immunisation, disease control, and strengthening health infrastructure and personnel. By improving public health care (particularly in rural areas), the NHM contributes to the health of the population — the health dimension of human capital formation. Understanding the National Health Mission (improving access to health care) is a prelims-relevant point. The National Health Mission aims to improve the availability of and access to quality health care, especially for the rural and poor population.

stem: Assertion (A): Investing in the health of the workforce is important for economic growth. Reason (R): A healthy worker is more productive, works more regularly (loses fewer days to illness), and can work for more years than an unhealthy one. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that investing in the health of the workforce is important for economic growth. And the reason is (R) that a healthy worker is more productive (can work harder and better), works more regularly (loses fewer working days to sickness), and can remain in the workforce for more years (a healthy person has a longer, more active working life) than an unhealthy worker. So, by making workers healthier, investment in health directly raises the quantity and quality of the labour they can supply — increasing productivity and output, and hence growth. Therefore R correctly explains why investing in health promotes growth (A). Understanding this link (health → productivity → growth) is a prelims point. Investing in workers' health promotes growth because a healthy worker is more productive, works more regularly, and works for more years than an unhealthy one.

stem: Human capital is the stock of __________ possessed by the people of a nation.
options: skill, education, knowledge and good health (embodied in people)
solution: Human capital is the stock of skill, expertise, knowledge and good health embodied in the people, which raises their productive capacity.

stem: A KEY difference between physical capital and human capital is that human capital:
options: can be separated from its owner
is inseparable from the person who possesses it (it cannot be sold separately)
solution: Physical capital (like a machine) can be sold separately, but human capital is inseparable from its owner — the person carries the skill and knowledge.

stem: Another difference is that physical capital is completely __________, while human capital is only partly so.
solution: Physical capital is fully mobile (it can be bought and moved anywhere), whereas human capital's mobility is restricted by nationality, culture and immigration rules.

stem: Human capital 'depreciates' with __________, whereas it can also appreciate (improve) with continuous education and use.
solution: Like physical capital, human capital depreciates with age (declining health/ability), but unlike machines it can appreciate through continuous learning and experience.

stem: Expenditure on education and health is regarded as an investment because it:
options: raises the future productivity and earning capacity of people
solution: Spending on education and health is an investment in human capital: it raises people's future productivity, incomes and quality of life, not merely a consumption expense.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a source of human capital formation?
options: Expenditure on luxury goods for consumption
solution: The sources of human capital formation are spending on education, health, on-the-job training, migration and acquiring information; luxury consumption is not a source.

stem: Expenditure on __________ is a source of human capital formation because it makes people fit and able to work more productively.
solution: Health expenditure (on preventive, curative and social medicine, water and sanitation) keeps the workforce fit, reducing illness and raising productivity — a key source of human capital.

stem: Migration is a source of human capital formation because people migrate in search of __________, which raises their earnings.
options: better job opportunities and higher salaries
solution: People migrate (internally or abroad) to seek better-paid jobs; the higher earnings, though involving migration costs, add to human capital formation.

stem: Spending to acquire __________ about the labour market and education is a source of human capital because it helps people make better decisions.
solution: Expenditure on acquiring information about labour markets, wages and educational institutions helps people use their human capital more efficiently, so it is a source of human capital formation.

stem: The two-way relationship between human capital and economic growth means that education/health promote growth, AND:
options: economic growth in turn provides more resources to invest in education and health
solution: Human capital raises growth, and higher growth generates the resources and demand to further invest in education and health — a virtuous cycle.

stem: 'On-the-job training' adds to human capital because it:
options: raises the skill and productivity of workers while they work
solution: On-the-job training (learning by doing, apprenticeships) enhances workers' skills and productivity, benefiting both the worker and the firm — an important source of human capital.

stem: Education and health are sometimes called __________ goods, so important that the government ensures their availability to all.
solution: Education and health are 'merit goods' — goods with large social benefits that the government provides/subsidises to ensure everyone, including the poor, can access them.

stem: A market failure argument for government intervention in education/health is that these have large __________ that private individuals do not fully capture.
solution: Education and health generate external benefits for society (e.g. a literate, healthy population benefits everyone), which the individual does not fully capture, so the market would under-provide them.

stem: In India, the ministry mainly responsible for EDUCATION is the Ministry of:
solution: Education in India is handled chiefly by the Ministry of Education (renamed in 2020 from the Ministry of Human Resource Development).

stem: The two regulatory bodies for maintaining standards in higher/technical education in India are the UGC and the:
options: AICTE (All India Council for Technical Education)
solution: The University Grants Commission (UGC) regulates universities/higher education, while the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) maintains standards in technical education.

stem: The regulatory body that looks after standards in MEDICAL education in India is the:
options: National Medical Commission (formerly Medical Council of India)
solution: Medical education standards are overseen by the National Medical Commission (which replaced the Medical Council of India).

stem: The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is a flagship programme aimed at achieving:
options: universal elementary education for children aged 6-14
solution: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan aims at universal elementary education (all children aged 6-14 in school), a key step in human capital formation.

stem: The Right to Education Act (2009) made free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children of which age group?
solution: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 guarantees free and compulsory education as a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14.

stem: The Mid-Day Meal Scheme, which provides free cooked meals in government schools, helps human capital formation by:
options: improving school attendance, retention and child nutrition
solution: The Mid-Day Meal Scheme improves enrolment, attendance and retention while also improving the nutrition and health of children — aiding education and health simultaneously.

stem: The Kothari (Education) Commission recommended that India should spend at least __________ of its GDP on education.
solution: The Kothari Commission (1964-66) recommended spending at least 6% of GDP on education; actual spending has generally remained below this.

stem: A tax specifically levied to raise funds for education in India is the:
solution: An 'education cess' is levied on payable taxes to raise additional resources for financing education, showing the government's effort to fund human capital formation.

stem: The proportion of the population enrolled at a particular level of education relative to the eligible age group is measured by the:
solution: The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) measures enrolment at a level of education as a percentage of the corresponding eligible age group.

stem: The proportion of students who leave school before completing a level is called the __________ rate, a serious problem in India.
solution: The dropout rate — the proportion of students leaving before completing a level — is a major challenge for Indian education and human capital formation.

stem: The education of WOMEN is considered especially important because it:
options: improves family health, child nutrition and education, and reduces fertility — benefiting the whole family and society
solution: Female education has powerful positive external effects — better family health, child care, education and lower fertility — so 'educating a woman educates a family'.

stem: 'Brain drain' refers to:
options: the emigration of highly educated and skilled persons from a developing country to developed countries
solution: Brain drain is the migration of skilled and educated people (doctors, engineers, scientists) from developing to developed countries, a loss of human capital for the home country.

stem: Although brain drain is a loss, emigrant skilled workers can benefit the home country by:
options: sending remittances, transferring technology/knowledge, and investing back home
solution: Skilled emigrants can benefit their home country through remittances, transfer of skills and technology, and investment — partly offsetting the brain drain.

stem: The 'demographic dividend' that India can reap from its large young population depends CRUCIALLY on:
options: investing adequately in the education, skills and health of the youth so they become productive
solution: India's demographic dividend (a large working-age population) will pay off only if the youth are educated, skilled and healthy; otherwise the large young population becomes a burden.

stem: The mission launched to train and enhance the employable skills of India's large youth population is the:
solution: The Skill India / National Skill Development Mission aims to train and skill India's youth to make them employable and productive.

stem: Education/training that imparts specific practical job skills for a trade or occupation is called __________ education.
solution: Vocational education provides specific occupational/trade skills (like plumbing, electrical work, computing), improving employability directly.

stem: The basic health-care institution serving rural India (the first point of contact for medical care) is the:
solution: The Primary Health Centre (PHC) is the basic rural health-care institution and the first point of contact for medical care in villages.

stem: Health services are of several kinds; providing vaccination and clean water/sanitation to prevent disease is called __________ medicine.
solution: Preventive medicine (like vaccination, safe water, sanitation) prevents disease, in contrast to curative medicine (treatment) and social medicine (health education/awareness).

stem: A concern about health care in India is the heavy reliance on __________ health expenditure, which burdens the poor.
solution: A large share of India's health spending is private out-of-pocket expenditure, which imposes a heavy and often catastrophic burden on poor families.

stem: The government scheme providing health insurance to poor families for hospital treatment (protecting them from catastrophic medical costs) is:
solution: Ayushman Bharat (Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana) provides health insurance/coverage to poor and vulnerable families for hospitalisation, reducing their health-cost burden.

stem: The key health indicators used to judge a population's health status include the infant mortality rate, life expectancy and the __________ rate.
solution: Health status is judged by indicators such as infant mortality rate, maternal mortality rate and life expectancy — all of which have improved since independence.

stem: Since independence, India's literacy rate has __________, though it has not yet become universal.
solution: India's literacy rate has risen substantially since 1947 (from about 16% to over 70%), but it is still not universal and gaps remain between men and women and rural and urban areas.

stem: The National Education Policy (NEP), which reformed India's education system from school to higher education, was announced in:
solution: The National Education Policy 2020 replaced the earlier 1986 policy, proposing wide-ranging reforms across school and higher education.

stem: In the human-DEVELOPMENT (as opposed to human-capital) view, education and health are treated as:
options: ends/goals in themselves that add to human well-being and freedom
solution: The human-development approach regards education and health as intrinsically valuable ends (adding to well-being and freedom), not merely as means to raise productivity.

stem: The human-development approach differs from the human-capital approach in that it values education/health even for a person whose:
options: education does not increase their productivity, because it still enhances their well-being
solution: In the human-development view, education and health are valuable even if they do not raise a person's productivity, since they directly improve human well-being and capabilities.

stem: A skilled and healthy workforce is important because it can better absorb and use __________, raising productivity.
solution: A skilled, healthy, educated workforce can adopt and effectively use new technology and modern production methods, raising productivity and growth.

stem: On-the-job training benefits the FIRM because:
options: the higher productivity of trained workers raises the firm's output and profits, outweighing the training cost
solution: Firms invest in on-the-job training because the resulting rise in worker productivity increases output and profit by more than the cost of the training.

stem: In India, expenditure on education is undertaken by:
options: both the central and state governments (and local bodies)
solution: Education spending in India is shared by the central and state governments (and local bodies), since education is on the Concurrent List.

stem: A market-related problem in human capital formation is that, because of imperfect information, individuals may __________ in their own education and health.
solution: Due to imperfect information (e.g. about the quality of schools/hospitals or future returns), and the external benefits they cannot capture, individuals tend to under-invest in education and health, justifying government support.

stem: Health of the population depends not only on medical care but also greatly on:
options: clean drinking water, sanitation, nutrition and a healthy environment
solution: Good health depends heavily on safe drinking water, sanitation, nutrition and a clean environment, in addition to curative medical care.

stem: The National (Rural) Health Mission aims to:
options: provide accessible, affordable and quality health care, especially to the rural and poor population
solution: The National Health Mission (including the National Rural Health Mission) aims to make quality health care accessible and affordable, especially for the rural and vulnerable population.

stem: A 'social benefit' (external benefit) of an educated society is that:
options: the whole society benefits — e.g. through a more informed citizenry, better civic participation and productivity
solution: An educated society yields external benefits — a more informed, participative citizenry, better governance and higher overall productivity — beyond the private gains to the individual.

stem: Investment in education raises a person's future __________, which is the PRIVATE benefit that motivates individuals to acquire education.
solution: Education raises a person's future earning capacity (income) — the private benefit that motivates individuals to invest in acquiring education.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter on human capital formation?
options: Only physical capital matters for growth
Investment in education and health builds human capital, which is essential for economic growth and human development, so it must be prioritised
solution: The chapter concludes that human capital (built through investment in education and health) is a crucial driver of both economic growth and human development, and hence deserves priority in policy.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Human Capital Formation in India' is that:
options: People are unimportant to the economy

Human capital — the education, skills, knowledge, and health of the people — is a vital resource for a country's growth and development; India must invest more in education and health (its main sources), overcoming challenges like inadequate spending, illiteracy, and brain drain, both to raise productivity and, above all, because human development (educated, healthy people) is a valuable end in itself
solution: The chapter conveys that human capital — the stock of education, skills, knowledge, expertise, and good health embodied in a country's people — is a vital resource for economic growth and development, alongside (and in some ways more important than) physical capital. It explains that human capital is built up through human capital formation — investment in the people, chiefly through education and health (the two main sources), and also through on-the-job training, migration, and information. Such spending on education and health should be seen as an investment (not a mere expense), because it raises people's productivity and future income, and human capital and growth reinforce each other in a virtuous cycle. The chapter also draws the important distinction between human capital (education/health as a means to higher production) and human development (education/health as valuable ends in themselves, essential to every person's well-being and right to a full life). It notes that, because education and health have large external/social benefits and the poor cannot afford them, the government must play a major role in providing and investing in them (as reflected in the Right to Education, and schemes like Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and the Mid-Day Meal). And it highlights the challenges facing human capital formation in India — inadequate spending on education and health, widespread illiteracy and poor-quality education, insufficient health facilities, and the 'brain drain' of skilled people abroad — which India must overcome to develop its human capital. Understanding what human capital is, how it is formed, its importance for growth AND for human development, the government's role, and the challenges in India, is the central concern of this chapter. Human capital — the education, skills, and health of the people — is vital both for growth and as an end in itself, so India must invest more in education and health and overcome challenges like inadequate spending, illiteracy, and brain drain.
